the core Operator::from_uri URI registry path, mirroring the Node.js

* refactor(bindings/python): simplify from_uri pickling and docs per review

- Drop the __from_uri field: reconstruct both scheme- and URI-built
  operators through a single from_uri-based reconstructor, since the core
  resolves bare schemes and full URIs through the same path.
- Reframe from_uri docstrings: options belong in the URI query string
  (urlencode example); **kwargs documented as override-only.

* docs(bindings/python): debloat from_uri docstrings and reconstructor comments

* docs(bindings/python): use fenced code block in from_uri examples

Replace >>> doctest prompts with a python code block so copying from the
rendered mkdocs docs does not include the prompt characters.

Split the single layers.rs into a src/layers/ package with one module per
layer plus a mod.rs holding the shared PythonLayer trait, the base Layer, and
re-exports. The Python surface stays flat on opendal.layers, so all existing
imports are unchanged and stub generation needs no special handling.

Adding a layer later is just: drop src/layers/<name>.rs, register it in
mod.rs and lib.rs, and run just stub-gen.

pull_request.title: fix(bindings/python): validate RetryLayer numeric inputs
pull_request.body:
RetryLayer accepted out-of-range values and forwarded them to the core
backoff builder, where they produce degenerate behavior: factor < 1.0
(or
NaN/inf) yields a nonsensical backoff, and negative/NaN max_delay or
min_delay silently clamp to zero via the f64->u64 cast.

Reject these at construction with ConfigInvalid: factor must be finite
and
>= 1.0; max_delay and min_delay must be finite and non-negative.
 Document
 the ranges and add tests covering the boundaries.

pull_request.body:
* feat(bindings/python): typed service configs via TypedDict

Generate one TypedDict per service into opendal/config.py, keyed on a
Literal scheme discriminant, plus a discriminated ServiceConfig union
consumed by a single Operator.from_config / AsyncOperator.from_config.

The TypedDicts are typing-only (defined under TYPE_CHECKING, resolved to
dict at runtime via __getattr__), so there is no runtime object, no
runtime dependency, and configs pickle trivially. from_config reads the
scheme key and converts native values (bool, int, os.PathLike, list) to
the flat string map core consumes.

Static checkers (mypy --strict, pyright, ty) catch a wrong scheme,
unknown/misspelled key, wrong value type, and missing required key
through both S3Config(...) and the from_config union.

* docs(bindings/python): render typed service configs

Add an api/config.md page (::: opendal.config) and a nav entry so the
generated *Config TypedDicts render in the API reference. mkdocstrings
reads the TYPE_CHECKING block via griffe static analysis; fields render
as attributes with types and docstrings, so no __new__/__init__ stub
rewrite is needed.

* chore(bindings/python): address review feedback on typed configs

- Define the *Config TypedDicts at runtime instead of hiding them under
  TYPE_CHECKING; drop the __getattr__ shim (a TypedDict is a dict at
  runtime). Required/NotRequired stay under TYPE_CHECKING so Python 3.10
  keeps working with no runtime typing_extensions dependency (annotations
  are strings via `from __future__ import annotations`).
- Drop the redundant `total=False` (every key is Required/NotRequired).
- Emit ruff-format-clean output (leading-pipe union, docstring code
  <=60 cols) so the check_generated CI job passes without a Python
  formatter step.
- Document both the call form and the annotated-variable form.

* fix(bindings/python): render config docstrings as markdown

mkdocstrings renders docstrings as markdown, so the reST `:meth:`/`:class:`
roles and the `::` literal block in the generated config module docstring
showed up literally. Switch to markdown: inline code refs and a fenced
```python block, and use single-backtick code spans in the class/field
docstrings.

pull_request.title: fix(services/gcs): stop double-encoding object paths in writer
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/gcs): stop double-encoding object paths in writer

The writer pre-encoded the path with gcs_percent_encode_path before
calling gcs_insert_object_request / gcs_initiate_multipart_upload, which
percent-encode again. A key like odfs/w/x.parquet was stored under the
literal name odfs%2Fw%2Fx.parquet and was unreadable, since the reader
encodes only once. Forward the raw path so it is encoded exactly once,
matching the reader and the other multipart calls.

Add regression tests asserting the write request single-encodes the path.

* fix(services/gcs): percent-encode path in multipart initiation

gcs_initiate_multipart_upload interpolated the object path into the URL
without percent-encoding, unlike gcs_upload_part / gcs_complete_multipart_upload
/ gcs_abort_multipart_upload. Once the writer forwards the raw path, object
names with characters that must be escaped (spaces, '#', non-ASCII, ...) would
produce an invalid or wrong initiation URI. Extract the request builder and
encode the path once, matching the other multipart calls.

Add a regression test asserting the initiation URI single-encodes the path.

* refactor(services/gcs): drop encoding-fix helpers per review

Address review feedback: remove the GcsWriter::insert_object_request
helper (inline into write_once), the build_test_core test constructor and
the request-builder unit tests that relied on it, and inline the
multipart-initiation request builder back into gcs_initiate_multipart_upload.

The source fixes are unchanged: the writer forwards the raw path and
gcs_initiate_multipart_upload percent-encodes the path once, matching the
other multipart helpers.

pull_request.body:
* feat(services/azblob): support if_match writes and honor preconditions on block commit

Azure Blob's Put Blob API supports If-Match with an arbitrary ETag, so wire
it in alongside the existing If-None-Match support and declare
write_with_if_match.

Conditional args were only applied to the single-shot Put Blob request.
Writing more than once before close() commits through Put Block + Put Block
List instead, and that commit request carried no conditional headers, so
if_match, if_none_match and if_not_exists were silently dropped and the
write degraded to an unconditional overwrite. Put Block does not evaluate
preconditions, so they are applied to Put Block List, which does.

Add behavior tests that force the block path by writing twice before
close(). They fail against Azurite on the previous code for if_none_match
and if_not_exists, and pass with this change.

pull_request.title: fix(core): Respect logical length in Buffer vectored views
pull_request.body:
`Buffer::to_io_slice` and the `bytes::Buf::chunks_vectored` impl walked
every underlying part to its physical end and ignored the logical `size`
field. Because `truncate`, `slice`, `split_to` and `split_off` shrink
`size` without dropping `parts`, both methods returned more bytes than
`remaining()` for a shortened non-contiguous buffer. That violates the
documented `chunks_vectored` contract and contradicts `chunk()` and
`Iterator::next`, which clamp with `.min(size)`.

Clamp both methods to the remaining logical length, mirroring `chunk()`.

pull_request.title: fix(services/cos): keep the port and stop doubling the bucket label
pull_request.body:
The request endpoint was composed from `Uri::host`, which omits the
port, so a custom endpoint such as https://cos.internal.example.com:8443
silently sent every request to 443. This is the same defect #4899 fixed
for OSS, and this follows that shape (`uri.port_u16()`).

The bucket-trim on the same line could never fire:

    uri.host().unwrap().replace(&format!("//{bucket}."), "//")

`Uri::host` never contains "//", so the pattern has no match by
construction, and an endpoint already carrying the bucket came out with
the label twice -- https://b.cos.example.com became
https://b.b.cos.example.com. Trimming a real prefix off the host fixes
that.

`uri.host().unwrap()` also panicked rather than reporting a
misconfiguration: both "/just/a/path" and "//cos.example.com" parse with
host = None. It now returns ConfigInvalid, matching how the same
function already reports an unparseable or empty endpoint.

The composition is extracted into build_endpoint so it can be asserted
on directly, mirroring S3Builder::build_endpoint.

Known limitation, unchanged here: COS always composes {bucket}.{host},
so an IP-based endpoint is still not usable -- http://127.0.0.1:9000
becomes http://bucket.127.0.0.1:9000. That needs an addressing-style
option like OSS and S3 have, which is a larger change.

Five tests. Three fail against the previous expression: the port case,
the doubled-bucket case, and the missing-host case. The other two --
plain bucket prefixing and the https default -- pass either way and are
there as controls.

pull_request.title: fix(services/upyun): do not panic when creating the service root
pull_request.body:
create_dir sliced the last byte off the absolute path to drop its
trailing slash:

    let path = build_abs_path(&self.root, path);
    let path = path[..path.len() - 1].to_string();

build_abs_path returns an empty string when the root is / and the path
is /, so path.len() - 1 underflows and the call panics with "attempt to
subtract with overflow" rather than returning a Result.

The root is reachable from the public API: Operator::create_dir only
rejects a path that does not end with /, and / does end with /, so
op.create_dir("/") on a default-rooted upyun operator panics inside the
library.

This was the only `len() - 1]` slice left in core/services; the sibling
services already use trim_end_matches('/') for this, which is total and
identical for a normalized path since normalize_path leaves exactly one
trailing slash.

Two unit tests. The root one panics against the previous expression;
the trailing-slash one passes either way, so it is a control rather
than a second copy of the same assertion.

pull_request.title: fix(services): percent-encode the pagination marker in list queries
pull_request.body:
QueryPairsWriter::push does no escaping of its own and says so:

    /// The input key and value must already been percent
    /// encoded correctly.

Five list builders hand it a raw marker. The value is whatever the
server returned as the resume point -- an object key for obs, cos and
swift, an opaque continuation token for azblob and azfile -- and for
swift's first page it is the user's own start_after argument, so no
pagination is needed to reach it.

Feeding the exact strings to http::Request::get shows what is sent:

    report 2024.csv   BUILD ERROR: invalid uri character
    a&b=c             marker=a  plus a stray b=c parameter
    note#1.txt        marker=note -- the rest is taken as a fragment
    AB+cd==           marker=AB+cd==, whose + a server decodes as a space

The middle two are the dangerous ones: the marker silently rewinds, the
server resends a page that was already delivered, and since done is
computed from the marker being empty the listing can repeat that page
indefinitely.

The repository already does this correctly in three places, one of them
in the same file as a site being fixed here:

    s3/src/core.rs:803    push("marker", &percent_encode_path(marker))
    cos/src/core.rs:606   push("key-marker", &percent_encode_path(key_marker))
    oss/src/core.rs:478   push("continuation-token", &percent_encode_path(token))

percent_encode_path is the right helper for a marker specifically: it
leaves `/` alone, which an object key needs. That is the difference from
#7888, which is encoding cos and tos versionId values in the same family
of defect and introduces a stricter set for them -- a version id is not
a path, a marker is.

No new tests. Each change is one call to a helper the file already

pull_request.title: fix(services/webhdfs): encode startAfter and abort the blocks that were written
pull_request.body:
Two independent path defects in this service.

1. The batched lister's startAfter is not encoded.

    let mut url = format!(
        "{}/webhdfs/v1/{}?op=LISTSTATUS_BATCH",
        self.endpoint,
        percent_encode_path(&p),      // the path is encoded
    );
    if !start_after.is_empty() {
        url += format!("&startAfter={start_after}").as_str();   // this is not
    }

start_after is ctx.token, which lister.rs sets verbatim from the last
entry's pathSuffix -- a raw HDFS file name. Measured against
http::Request::get: a name with a space is a hard "invalid uri
character" build error, one with # truncates the marker so the batch
boundary rewinds and a page repeats, and one with & grafts a stray
parameter onto the query.

This is the same defect just fixed for the marker parameter across
obs/swift/cos/azblob/azfile in #8073; it was out of that PR's scope only
because it is a format! concatenation rather than a QueryPairsWriter
push. startAfter is the one query value in this file carrying data the
server chose. user.name is config, at eleven sites, and is a separate
question; &{auth} is deliberately a whole query fragment and must stay
verbatim.

2. abort_block deletes paths that were never written.

write_block creates each block at {atomic_write_dir}{block_id} and
complete_block concatenates from the same strings, but abort_block asked
for {block_id} alone. So aborting a multi-block write -- Writer::abort,
or any mid-write failure -- deleted a path that does not exist and left
every uploaded block sitting in atomic_write_dir for ever.

It now resolves atomic_write_dir the same way write_block does, which
also makes the unsupported case explicit rather than deleting a
top-level path named after a UUID.

No new tests: both are single expressions inside async methods whose
seams are an HTTP round trip, and asserting on either would mean
restructuring the URL builder and the writer. The seven existing unit
tests pass, fmt and clippy are clean.

pull_request.title: fix(services/gridfs): default the chunk size to 255 KiB, not 255 bytes
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/gridfs): default the chunk size to 255 KiB, not 255 bytes

GridfsBuilder::chunk_size documents "Default to `255 KiB` if not
specified", and the value is handed to GridFsBucketOptions:

    let chunk_size = self.config.chunk_size.unwrap_or(255);
    ...
    .chunk_size_bytes(Some(self.chunk_size))

chunk_size_bytes is measured in bytes -- mongodb 3.6.0 spells it out in
gridfs/options.rs:20, "The chunk size in bytes used to break the user
file into chunks. Defaults to 255 KiB", and backs it with

    const DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES: u32 = 255 * 1024;   // gridfs.rs:27

So an operator built without an explicit chunk_size gets 255-byte
chunks: 1024x smaller than this builder's own rustdoc promises and than
the driver would have chosen. A 1 MiB object is stored as 4112 chunk
documents instead of 5, on the default configuration path that needs no
options at all.

The default moves into a named constant next to the builder, and the
one-line resolution behind resolve_chunk_size so the default is
assertable without a live MongoDB.

Explicitly configured sizes were always correct and stay untouched;
existing data is unaffected, since GridFS records chunkSize per file and
reads use the stored value rather than the bucket option.

Two unit tests. Putting 255 back fails the default test; the
pass-through test holds either way.

* Address review: inline the default and drop the helper

Review points from @erickguan, all applied:

- constant doc shortened to one line, with the KiB spelled in a trailing
  comment
- resolve_chunk_size removed; the default is applied inline at the call
  site
- test module removed, since it only exercised that helper
- builder rustdoc reworded

The change is now the named constant plus the one call site.

One deviation from the suggestion, flagged rather than silently applied:
the trailing comment says "255 KiB" instead of "255KB". 255 * 1024 is
261120 bytes, which is KiB; the rustdoc three lines above already says
KiB, so KB would have been inconsistent inside the same file.

pull_request.title: fix(services/d1): repair the upsert statement that breaks every write
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/d1): repair the upsert statement that breaks every write

The statement built in D1Core::set carries two defects, and either one
alone is enough to stop a write from landing.

It is a raw string, so the three trailing backslashes are literal
backslash characters rather than line continuations. SQLite stops at the
first one:

  sqlite> INSERT INTO "data" ("key", "value") \
  Parse error near line 1: unrecognized token: "\"

And the key placeholder is quoted. 'val' is a string literal in SQL, so
'?' is the one-character string "?" rather than a bind marker. That
leaves a single placeholder for the two parameters set always sends, and
every row lands under the literal key "?":

  sqlite> INSERT INTO "data" ("key","value") VALUES ('?','hello') ...
  sqlite> SELECT '['||key||'] -> '||value FROM data;
  [?] -> hello

Both arrived together in 311f324cc (#7857), which rewrote the literal as
a raw string in order to quote the table and column identifiers:

  -  "INSERT INTO {table} ({key_field}, {value_field}) \
  -      VALUES (?, ?) \
  +  r#"INSERT INTO "{table}" ("{key_field}", "{value_field}") \
  +      VALUES ('?', ?) \

The identifier quoting that change was after is kept; only the escaping
and the placeholder are corrected. The statement moves into a
build_set_query helper so it can be asserted on directly.

The rest of the crate is unaffected: delete and the two SELECTs are
single-line raw strings with bare `?`, and a sweep for the shape --
a raw string with a line-ending backslash -- finds no other occurrence
in the repository.

One observation left out of this change, for a maintainer to judge
separately: set matches on the HTTP status alone, while get and
get_length both run D1Response::parse. D1 answers a rejected statement
with 200 and success:false, so the parse error above was reported to
callers as a successful write. That is why a service whose every write
fails has no bug report against it.

Two unit tests. Restoring either defect on its own fails
set_query_binds_both_parameters; the second test pins the identifier
quoting and passes against both the old and the new statement, so it
holds the #7857 intent in place.

* Address review: inline the statement and drop the test module

Review points from @erickguan, both applied:

- build_set_query removed; the format! goes back inline at the call
  site, with the same local bindings the original had
- test module removed

The diff against main is now three lines: the three literal backslashes
go, and the key placeholder loses its quotes.

pull_request.title: fix(services/vercel-blob): send the pagination cursor so listing terminates
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/vercel-blob): send the pagination cursor so listing terminates

The lister stores the cursor the server returns:

    ctx.done = !resp.has_more;

    if let Some(cursor) = resp.cursor {
        ctx.token = cursor;
    }

and nothing ever reads it back. VercelBlobCore::list took only a prefix
and a limit, so page two was byte-identical to page one:

    https://blob.vercel-storage.com?prefix={prefix}&limit={limit}

ctx.token is the only write of that field in the crate. Meanwhile
PageLister::next loops while ctx.done is false, so a listing the server
truncates never advances: the same page is fetched and pushed again for
as long as has_more stays true. Operator::list collects into a Vec and
grows without bound; lister() streams the same entries forever.

Vercel documents cursor beside prefix and limit -- "a string obtained
from a previous list response to be used for reading the next page of
results" -- and the default limit is 1000, so any prefix holding more
than that reaches this without the caller setting anything.

list now takes the cursor and appends it when non-empty, and the URL
construction moves into build_list_url so it can be asserted directly.
The four internal lookups pass "": each asks for Some(1) to resolve a
single blob's URL and never paginates.

One extra guard in the lister: has_more true with no cursor now ends the
listing rather than leaving ctx.done false. That truncates, but the only
other option is re-requesting the same page indefinitely.

Four unit tests. Dropping the cursor from the URL again fails exactly
the two that involve one; the first-page and root-prefix tests hold
either way.

* Address review: Option<&str> cursor, inline the URL, drop the tests

Review points from @erickguan, all three applied:

- cursor is Option<&str> rather than an empty string standing in for
  "no cursor"; the four single-blob lookups pass None, and the lister
  turns an empty ctx.token into None
- build_list_url removed, the format! goes back inline
- test module removed

The functional change is unchanged: the cursor is sent when there is
one, percent-encoded because it is an opaque server token.

pull_request.title: fix(services/ipmfs): stop stripping the root twice from listed entries
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/ipmfs): stop stripping the root twice from listed entries

The listing loop concatenates the path being listed with a files/ls
name, then runs the result through build_rel_path a second time:

    let path = match object.mode() {
        EntryMode::FILE => format!("{}{}", self.path, object.name),
        ...
    };
    let path = build_rel_path(&self.root, &path);

self.path is what the operator handed the service, so it is already
relative to the root -- IpmfsCore::ipmfs_ls is what turns it into a
rooted absolute path for the request. The concatenation is therefore
root-relative before that call, and the call removes a prefix that is
not there.

Under the default root "/" the second strip happens to cancel out, which
is why this has gone unnoticed. Under any other root, in release:

    root "/abc/", listing "dir/", name "a"
        build_rel_path("/abc/", "dir/a") -> "a"
        the directory is dropped from every entry path

    root "/abc/", listing the root itself (self.path is "/"), name "a"
        build_rel_path("/abc/", "/a")
        panicked: start byte index 5 is out of bounds for string of
        length 2

In a debug build both cases trip the debug_assert! inside build_rel_path
instead.

The construction moves into build_entry_path, which takes no root at
all -- an entry path does not depend on one. The only thing it has to
handle is that self.path is "/" when the root itself is listed, and an
entry path carries no leading slash.

The self-entry twenty lines above is left alone: it does
build_abs_path then build_rel_path, a deliberate round trip, and is
correct.

Three unit tests. Putting the old expression back passes all of them
with a root of "/" and fails three of them with a root of "/abc/" --
which is the shape of the bug.

Note for rebasing: #7801 renames this very call to
build_relative_path. If that lands first this needs a one-word rebase;
the call itself goes away here.

* Inline the entry-path construction and drop the test module

Matching the shape asked for on #8068, #8069 and #8071 rather than
waiting to be asked again: the extracted helper goes, the construction
is inline, and the test module goes with it.

The fix is unchanged -- the concatenation is already relative to the
root, so the second build_rel_path is what truncated it, and "/" as the
listed path must not become a leading slash on the entry.

* Drop the inline comment

pull_request.title: fix(services/dbfs): root the put path and stop encoding paths in JSON bodies
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/dbfs): root the put path and stop encoding paths in JSON bodies

Two defects in how this service addresses paths, both in core.rs.

The path in the dbfs/put body is not rooted:

    let req_body = &json!({
        "path": path,

Every sibling roots it first -- create_dir at :60, delete at :89,
rename at :116, list at :142, get-status at :193 all call
build_rooted_abs_path. The value arrives from DbfsBackend::write as the
operator-relative path and nothing else applies the root, so with any
non-default root a write and the stat, list or delete that follows it
address different DBFS paths.

And four values are percent-encoded inside JSON request bodies:

    "path": percent_encode_path(&p),                     // :65, :94
    "source_path": percent_encode_path(&source),         // :126
    "destination_path": percent_encode_path(&target),    // :127

Nothing URL-decodes a JSON string value. The genuine query strings at
:149 and :200 are encoded, and the server does decode those -- so the
two halves of this file disagree with each other. create_dir("my dir/")
creates a directory literally named my%20dir, while the get-status that
follows asks for "my dir" and gets NotFound. For delete it is worse than
an error: deleter.rs notes the server answers 200 even when the path
does not exist, so the call reports success having removed nothing.

A repo-wide grep for percent_encode_path inside json! across
core/services matches these four lines and nothing else; dbfs is the
only service in the tree that does it.

Neither change affects an ordinary path. percent_encode_path leaves
A-Z a-z 0-9 / - _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) untouched, so a plain key serialises
identically; only a path containing a space, %, #, ?, &, +, ,, :, =, @
or a non-ASCII byte changes, and those are the ones broken today.

One test, on the only one of the four that is a synchronous request
builder. The other three send inside async methods, so pinning them
would mean restructuring; their evidence is the in-file inconsistency
above. Reverting the rooting fails that test and nothing else.

The lister emits root-prefixed entry paths as well -- that is a separate
change to a separate file and is not in here.

Note for rebasing: #7801 renames build_rooted_abs_path in this file. If
it lands first the new call in dbfs_create_file_request needs the new
name.

* Remove the test module

fix(services/github): do not double the separator in recursive listings
pull_request.body:
The native-recursive branch joins the listed path with the tree entry:

    format!("{}/{}", self.path, t.path)

self.path is the path the operator passed in, normalized, so it keeps
its trailing slash. list_with("src/").recursive(true) therefore emits
src//services/mod.rs. Nothing downstream removes the doubled separator
-- oio::Entry::with only rewrites the empty string to "/" -- so the user
sees it.

The no-trailing-slash form, list_with("src"), comes out right, which
means the natural way to name a directory is the one that breaks. The
non-recursive branch sixteen lines above uses build_rel_path and does
not have the problem, so the two branches disagree with each other.

Trimming the trailing slash before the join fixes the slash form and
leaves the other one byte-identical. The self.path == "/" case keeps its
own branch, since trimming there would give a leading slash instead.

pull_request.title: fix(services/sqlite): match the directory prefix exactly instead of with LIKE
fix(services/pcloud): send the service root as / rather than empty
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/pcloud): send the service root as / rather than empty

list_folder is the only method in this file that formats path={} rather
than path=/{}, and the only one that runs the value through
normalize_root first. For the service root the two differences cancel
out everywhere except the default root, where they leave the parameter
empty:

    root "/",      list("/")   ->  path=          (stat sends path=/)
    root "/",      list("a/")  ->  path=/a        (same as before)
    root "/data/", list("/")   ->  path=/data     (same as before)

build_abs_path returns root[1..] when the path is "/", so with the
default root that is the empty string; normalize_root turns it back into
"/" and trim_end_matches then removes it again.

Dropping the normalize_root hop and using the path=/{} form the other
ten call sites use makes the root case agree with stat and leaves every
other input byte-identical.

* Special-case the root instead of dropping normalize_root

Review feedback: removing normalize_root also removed its collapsing of
empty path segments, so a path with an interior // would have produced a
different URL. That was outside the blast radius the PR claimed.

Keep normalize_root and substitute / when trimming leaves nothing, which
touches only the case this PR is about.

* Drop the comment

pull_request.title: fix(services/ipfs): address listed children by their full path
pull_request.body:
The links in a dag-pb node are bare names -- one path segment each. The
lister passed them straight to ipfs_stat, which roots whatever it is
given with build_rooted_abs_path, so listing a subdirectory statted the
wrong object: /ipfs/CID/x.txt for a child of /ipfs/CID/dir/. Usually a
404 that fails the whole listing, or, if a same-named object exists at
the root, silently the wrong metadata. The entry path pushed to the
caller lost its directory the same way.

self.path is what the operator handed the service -- ipfs_list roots it
for the request -- so prefixing the name with it yields the path both
calls need. It already carries its trailing slash.

ipfs declares list but not list_with_recursive, so SimulateLayer drives
recursion by re-entering list for each directory it finds; a recursive
listing from the root reaches this on the first subdirectory.

Listing the operator root is unchanged: self.path is "/" there, the
child is the bare name, and that is what was sent before.

azblob declares write_with_content_type and write_with_user_metadata, but
only azblob_put_blob_request honours them, and BlockWriter reaches that
only for a one-shot write. A chunked write commits through Put Block List,
which set cache-control and the conditional headers but neither the content
type nor x-ms-meta-*, so both were dropped.

there looked like coverage without being any.

pull_request.title: fix(services/memcached): reject a TTL over 30 days
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/memcached): send a TTL over 30 days as an absolute expiry

memcached reads an expiration larger than 60*60*24*30 as an absolute Unix
timestamp rather than an offset from now. default_ttl was passed straight
through as as_secs() as u32, so a TTL of, say, 60 days went out as 5184000,
which the server read as a moment in February 1970 -- already past. The store
succeeds and the item is gone, with nothing logged.

Convert such a TTL to now + ttl, which is how memcached will read it, and
saturate rather than wrap at u32::MAX. A TTL of 30 days or less is unchanged.

* Reject a TTL over 30 days instead of converting it

Per review: refuse the value at build time rather than silently rewriting it
into memcached's absolute form.

fix(services/hf): cache XET classification and CAS auth tokens
pull_request.body:
* fix(services/hf): cache XET classification and CAS auth tokens

Every ranged read of an HF bucket/dataset file independently called
HfCore::resolve() to learn the file's XET hash, and independently built a
fresh XetDownloadStreamGroup/XetUploadCommit, each of which eagerly
fetches its own CAS auth token on creation. For N ranges into one file
read through a single Reader (e.g. object_store::get_ranges), this meant
N /resolve requests and N CAS token-refresh /api requests instead of one
each, tripping HF's resolver and API rate limits -- the /api quota (3k/5m)
first, since it's smaller than the resolver quota (20k/5m).

HfReader now caches the learned (hash, size) and the resulting
XetDownloadStreamGroup for its own lifetime, single-flighted via
asyncband::OnceCell so concurrent opens (object_store defaults to 8-way
concurrency) share one classification instead of each resolving
independently. Non-XET files are unaffected -- there's no separate
metadata step to skip for them, so every range still fetches its own
bytes, at the cost of one extra one-time probe request per reader (its
response can't be reused once several concurrent callers might have
raced to produce it).

Separately, HfCore now fetches and caches its own CAS read/write tokens
via opendal's normal HTTP transport, refreshing 120s ahead of real expiry,
and seeds every new XetDownloadStreamGroup/XetUploadCommit from that
cache instead of letting them discover a token lazily through the xet
crate's own, separate HTTP client. This is shared across the whole
Operator, so unlike the per-Reader hash/group cache above, it also
collapses token requests across different files, not just repeated ranges
of one file.

The CAS group/commit objects themselves stay scoped to HfReader/HfWriter
rather than being cached on HfCore alongside the token: XetDownloadStreamGroup's
internal per-item progress tracking has no eviction, so sharing one for an
Operator's entire lifetime would leak memory proportional to every file
ever read.

Adds core/services/hf/examples/blob_range_repro.rs, a small opendal-only
(no lancedb) reproducer that demonstrates the fix live against a public
HF dataset: N independent single-range reads vs. one Reader batching all N
ranges vs. a second Reader simulating a different file, with request
counts by endpoint.

Verified live: 16 ranges into one file dropped from 16 resolve + 16
token requests to 1 of each; a second Reader on a different file reused
the cached token instead of fetching its own.

* test(services/hf): cover cached-token reuse, XET single-flight, and retry-after-failure

Adds tests that exercise xet_download_group/xet_upload_commit through the
real cache-reuse path, concurrent cold opens on a XET-backed file sharing
one classifying resolve and one xet_group build, the refresh-buffer
boundary condition, and retry behavior after a failed token/classifying
request.

* fix(services/hf): tag XET write-token fetch as Operation::Write, dedup canonical_repo lookup

`cached_xet_token` hardcoded `Operation::Read` regardless of scope, so a
write-token fetch skipped the local `PermissionDenied` fast-path for
token-less writers and instead fired an unauthenticated network call.
`xet_auth` also resolved `canonical_repo` a second time on every call even
though `cached_xet_token` already resolved it internally.

- Tag the token request with `XetTokenScope::operation()` so write-scope
  fetches are rejected locally without a token, matching every other write
  path.
- Thread the already-resolved `HfRepo` from `xet_auth` into
  `cached_xet_token` instead of looking it up twice; this also shrinks the
  token mutex's critical section to just the token HTTP call.
- Factor `HfReader::open()`'s "classify resolve response, dispatch to
  xet_stream/new_http" step into `dispatch()`, shared by the Http-mode
  branch.
- Remove `examples/blob_range_repro.rs`: an unasserted manual repro that
  duplicates coverage already in `core.rs`'s test suite.
- Add a debug log in `HfCore::request()` (the shared entry point for every
  outbound HF/CAS request) so `RUST_LOG=opendal_service_hf::core=debug`
  shows what's actually being queried.
- Add tests: a token-less write-commit rejection test, and a test pinning
  today's known-but-unfixed behavior where a single-flighted XET
  classification's Range header comes from whichever concurrent caller
  wins the race.

AI-assisted: findings from a multi-angle automated review of the prior two
commits on this branch were manually verified and selectively applied.

pull_request.body:
`GoosefsBuilder::build()` overlaid `master_addr` on top of the config that
`from_properties_auto()` had already resolved, so the URI authority of
`goosefs://host:port/path` (or the `master_addr` option) always won and the

`goosefs-site.properties` never reached the client. A client pointed at a site
file that lists the real HA masters still dialed the URI authority and failed
with a gRPC transport error.

`build()` now resolves master addresses as `GOOSEFS_MASTER_ADDR` >
`goosefs-site.properties` > `master_addr`. The site file outranks
`master_addr` because it carries a deployment's whole HA master list, which a
single URI authority cannot express, and `GOOSEFS_MASTER_ADDR` stays on top as
the per-process override. Because `from_properties_auto()` falls back to the
SDK default `127.0.0.1:9200`, the builder now asks which source actually
declared an address instead of reading the loaded value.

User-facing impact: a site file or `GOOSEFS_MASTER_ADDR` now supersedes the URI
authority and the `master_addr` option, and `build()` fails with
`ConfigInvalid` when no source supplies an address instead of silently dialing
`127.0.0.1:9200`.

Bump goosefs-sdk to 0.1.9 for RUSTSEC-2026-0002 (`lru` >= 0.16.3) and master
connection pooling. 0.1.9 does not yet honor `$GOOSEFS_CONF_DIR`;
`$GOOSEFS_CONFIG_FILE` remains the way to point at a file outside the searched
directories. Regenerated Java, .NET, and website docs for the new
`master_addr` precedence.

pull_request.title: fix(services/hf): follow case redirects instead of resolving the canonical repo id
pull_request.body:
#8108 fixed writes against a repo id that differs in case from the
canonical one (#8107) by fetching repo-info on first use and building every
URL from the returned id. That costs each Operator an extra /api request and
made URL construction async.

Replace it with HfCore::send, which re-issues a request once when HF answers
307/308 with a Location on the configured endpoint. Other hosts are not
followed, so the bearer token stays on the endpoint, and the refused
redirect is named in the error.

Also trim a trailing slash from the resolved endpoint, as azblob, azdls,
azfile, alluxio and cloudflare-kv already do. Every URL is built by
appending `/api/...` to it, so `HF_ENDPOINT=https://huggingface.co/`
produced `//api/...`, which HF answers with 404. Normalizing there also
lets `send` compare the Location against the endpoint directly instead of
picking the origin out of it.

Verified live against huggingface.co with an upper-cased dataset id: the
stock reqwest transport follows the GET redirects itself but hands bodied
POSTs (commit, paths-info) back as bare 307s, which is the #8107 failure.
With send, write, stat, read and delete succeed in both download modes.

pull_request.title: fix(services/hf): pin the xet probe range and drop dead http-mode classification
pull_request.body:
In `xet` mode every read first asks `/resolve` whether the path is
XET-backed, with `Accept: application/vnd.xet-fileinfo+json`. That probe sent
the caller's range. For a XET-backed path HF answers with a 441-byte metadata
document whatever the range, but for a path that is *not* XET-backed the
accept header is ignored and the body is the file content -- so a caller
asking for a full read made the probe download the whole file and discard it
(248,987 B on one measured file). It now sends `Range: bytes=0-0`, which HF
documents as a header parameter, capping that to one byte. Pinning it also
makes the request deterministic rather than dependent on which concurrent
open() won the single-flight race.

Http mode no longer classifies its resolve response. It sends no accept
header, so HF returns the content itself; the XET arm was unreachable, and a
response that did carry the header would have hit the JSON parser. The
one-caller `dispatch` wrapper goes with it.

Keeps reading the response body rather than the `x-xet-hash` /
`x-linked-size` headers: HF's OpenAPI spec defines the body with `hash` and
`size` as required fields, while those headers appear nowhere in it.

pull_request.title: fix(services/hf): drop the trailing slash from the root tree URL
pull_request.body:
`HfUri::file_tree_url` always appended the path separator, so listing the
repo root -- where the path is empty -- asked for `tree/main/` on a git repo
and `tree/` on a bucket. HF answers both with a 302 to the slash-less URL, so
every root listing paid an extra round trip on the rate-limited /api class,
and failed outright on a transport configured not to follow redirects.

Append the separator only for a non-empty path. Verified live against
huggingface.co: `tree/main/?expand=True` and `buckets/<id>/tree/?expand=True`
both return 302, while the slash-less forms return 200, and a subdirectory
listing is unaffected. The same holds for a percent-encoded revision:
`tree/refs%2Fconvert%2Fparquet` returns 200 and its trailing-slash form
returns 302, so decoding the ref back into path segments does not depend on a
terminating slash. With the fix, listing the root of a dataset and of a bucket
each complete in one request with redirects disabled.

An empty revision reached the same broken URL by a second route. `revision()`
falls back to `main` only for `None`, so a `Some("")` built `tree/` and, with
a path, `tree//data`. Normalize it in `HfRepo::new`, the one constructor every
call site funnels through: `hf://datasets/user/repo@` reaches it from
`HfUri::parse`, and `revision=""` reaches it from `HfConfig::from_uri` through
`HfBuilder::build`, which passes the option through unchecked. Normalizing at
the constructor covers both and lets the pre-existing guard in the sibling
parse branch go away, since no caller can construct the state any more.

Pin the URL shapes with direct `file_tree_url` assertions next to the existing
`test_bucket_*_url` tests: git and bucket roots, both subdirectory forms, an
encoded revision, and the recursive/cursor query. The function is a pure
string builder, so these need no mock transport.
